extracted.intended_audience: general readers and fans researching John Cleese and British comedy
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia biography page about John Cleese covering his comedy style, public statements on political correctness and satire, activism, personal life, and career highlights. Extracts principles and positions he has expressed about humour and its social role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black humour as a comedic approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleese explained the origin of his fondness for 'black humour' and lists examples (Dead Parrot sketch, 'The Kipper and the Corpse', Undertakers sketch, his eulogy at Graham Chapman which included 'Good riddance to him, the freeloading bastard! I hope he fries.'). He states 'I can take almost nothing seriously'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of morbid or dark themes as a deliberate comic device; examples demonstrate deploying shock, morbidity or irreverence to produce laughter. Indicates an attitude of treating serious subjects with absurdity rather than solemnity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context matters in humour ('words depend on their context')
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleese: 'The main thing is to realise that words depend on their context [...] PC people simply don't understand this business about context because they tend to be very literal-minded.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or writing jokes, consider the surrounding context—character, framing, and authorial intent—because identical words can have different meanings depending on context. Literal-minded censorship that ignores context can misread satirical targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political correctness/wokeism can stifle creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleese has criticised political correctness and wokeism, saying that despite initial good intentions to 'not be mean to people', they have become 'a sort of indulgence of the most over-sensitive people in your culture... if you have to keep thinking which words you can use and which you can't, then that will stifle creativity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle that excessive policing of language and over-sensitivity may limit comedians' creative freedom and risk producing bland, unchallenging material. Balancing empathy and creative risk-taking is key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should mock and discredit objectionable views by clearly targeting them
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleese likened Fawlty Towers' humour to the representation of Alf Garnett: 'We laughed at Alf's reactionary views. Thus we discredited them, by laughing at him. Of course, there were people—very stupid people—who said 'Thank God someone is saying these things at last'. We laughed at these people too.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective satirical comedy frames characters or views as objects of ridicule so the audience understands the target of the joke is the hateful or reactionary view itself. Clarity of target prevents misinterpretation as endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent and framing justify depiction of offensive material
rubrics_metrics.description: In defending the Fawlty Towers episode 'The Germans', Cleese argued the programme 'was mocking prejudice' through a character who utters racial slurs—implying that the intent to satirise prejudice is relevant to whether material is acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including offensive language or behavior in comedy, ensure the overall framing makes the critical intent explicit so the audience perceives it as condemnation rather than celebration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire's purpose: to make people think
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted in interview summaries: Cleese (and cited interviews) express the view that 'satire makes people think' and that satirical work should provoke reflection rather than merely offend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for satirical content that encourages critical reflection and discussion; success is measured by whether it prompts thought about the target or issue, not merely shock value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comedy as a tool for activism and fundraising
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleese instigated the Secret Policeman's Ball benefit shows for Amnesty International in 1976 and used comedy ensembles and celebrity participation to raise funds and awareness for human rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy can be mobilised for charitable or political causes; leverage star power and ensemble performance to attract attention and inspire broader activism. Historical example demonstrates cultural influence beyond entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morbid humour can be effective in public-health messaging (limited effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1992 anti-smoking PSAs featuring Cleese used sketches 'rife with morbid humour' designed to encourage adult smokers to quit; a controlled study estimated the campaign would reduce smoking prevalence by about 1.2% over 18 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using dark or morbid comedic elements in behaviour-change campaigns can produce measurable (though modest) effects. Consider target population, region, and combination with other interventions; do not assume large effect sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative decisions should be made by creators, not risk-averse bureaucrats
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleese criticised the BBC as being 'run by a mixture of marketing people and petty bureaucrats' whose main concern is 'not losing their jobs'—leading to 'cowardly and gutless' decisions affecting comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve creator involvement in editorial decisions to maintain comedic integrity; over-management by non-creative administrators can lead to overcautious content choices that dilute humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive audience-sensitivity/pandering reduces comedic effectiveness ('woke joke... might be heart-warming but it's not going to be very funny')
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleese suggested a 'woke joke [...] might be heart-warming but it's not going to be very funny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material that prioritises pleasing all sensibilities or seeks to avoid offending at all costs risks becoming sentimental and losing sharpness or comedic impact. Strive for boldness balanced with responsible framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect freedom of thought and expression for comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleese has argued that political correctness and wokeism are a threat to humour, creativity, and 'freedom of thought and expression.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain legal and normative protections for free expression to allow satire and comedy to critique society. When evaluating comedic work, consider whether constraints on expression are limiting its ability to challenge ideas.
